deed: אליעזר אשכנזי הקים בצפת את בית הדפוס העברי הראשון בארץ ישראל
title: A Jewish printer from Prague brought type to Safed and printed there the first book in the Land of Israel

trailer.text: According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, Eliezer ben Isaac Ashkenazi was a 16th-century Hebrew printer, born in Prague.
According to Marvin Heller, he was an Eastern European Jew, a wandering printer who worked for several decades in Lublin, Constantinople and Safed.

According to Heller, in Safed he set up a press with Abraham ben Isaac Ashkenazi, a resident of the town: Eliezer brought the expertise and the typographic material, and Abraham provided the location and the financing.
According to a Times of Israel blog, the book 'Lekach Tov', printed there in 1577, is the first book printed in the Land of Israel.

According to the blog, the press produced only six books up to 1587 and closed, and in 1977 a facsimile edition of 'Lekach Tov' was issued to mark four hundred years since the first Hebrew book printed in the Land of Israel.

paragraphs.text: According to Marvin Heller, Eliezer was a well-known printer from Prague, and possibly a grandson of Hayyim Shahor.
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, he printed Hebrew books in Lublin, with partners, between 1557 and 1573.
According to Heller, his first imprint there was a Pentateuch with Rashi, the Scrolls and Haftarot, completed on 18 October 1557.
According to the Encyclopaedia, an epidemic forced him to move for a short while to Konska Wola, near Lublin.
According to Heller, at that time he did not yet call himself 'Ashkenazi'.
According to Heller, he printed his last book in Lublin, 'Pahad Yizhak', in 1573.
According to Heller, Eliezer entered into partnership with Kashti because he did not have the money to buy paper.
According to the Israel in Their Land website, he operated a Hebrew printing press in Constantinople for approximately three years.

According to Heller, a well-established Hebrew press was already operating in Constantinople at the time, and Eliezer and his son arrived there as skilled craftsmen whose skills were useful but not essential.
According to Heller, it was there that he first used the surname 'Ashkenazi'.
According to Heller, Kashti, dissatisfied with the Jabez brothers, gave Eliezer the second volume of the mahzor to print.
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, the partnership broke up before the mahzor was finished, and Eliezer alone printed 'Mekor Barukh' in 1576.

stations.title: On the way to Safed, and a new partner

paragraphs.text: According to the Times of Israel blog, 16th-century Safed was a thriving center of Jewish life in the Land of Israel, and part of a wider Sephardic world.
According to the Jerusalem Post, in the mid-century Safed was the largest Jewish center in the country, and home to sages and kabbalists such as Rabbi Joseph Karo and the Ari.
According to Heller, after 'Mekor Baruch' Eliezer and his son Isaac left for Safed.
According to Israel in Their Land, he moved to Safed because of stiff competition in Constantinople.
According to Heller, the partner in Safed, Abraham ben Isaac Ashkenazi, was a resident of the town whom Eliezer had met in Constantinople, and he was an emissary of the Tiberias Yeshivah.
According to Heller, Eliezer brought the expertise and the typographic material, and Abraham provided the location and the financing.
According to Heller, Eliezer most likely did all of the work himself, since no other name is mentioned in the books.
According to Heller, the first book printed at the Safed press, in 1577, was 'Lekah Tov'.
According to the Times of Israel blog, it is a commentary on the Book of Esther, and it is the first book printed in the Land of Israel.
According to the blog, the book was written by the young scholar Yom Tov Tzahalon, who was born in Safed to a family of Spanish exiles who had resettled in the Galilee.
According to Heller, Tzahalon wrote in the introduction that the Lord roused the heart of the printer Eliezer, and so honor dwelled in our land.
According to the blog, on the back of the title page Tzahalon urged other local authors to have their books printed in Safed rather than abroad.
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, between 1577 and 1579 Eliezer and Abraham printed three works.

According to Heller, the largest book Eliezer printed in Safed was 'Kehillat Ya'akov': according to the title page, printing began on 15 November 1577, and it was completed on 23 August 1578, nine and a half months later.
According to Israel in Their Land, the book 'Sar Shalom' by Shmuel Arepol was printed in Safed in 1579 by Abraham and Eliezer Ashkenazi.
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, Eliezer later returned to Constantinople and printed 'Lev Hakham' there in 1586, again with Kashti.
According to the Encyclopaedia, in 1587 he printed three more books in Safed, and he apparently died soon after.
According to the Times of Israel blog, between 1577 and 1587 only six books came out of the press, and then it closed.

According to 'Israel in Their Land', the difficulties included economic instability in Tsfat, to which were added Ottoman hardships and competition from the well-established Hebrew presses of Constantinople and Venice.

stations.title: What remains: first in the Land and in the East

paragraphs.text: According to the Times of Israel blog, modern scholarship generally describes 'Lekach Tov' as the first book printed in the Land of Israel, and as the first Hebrew book printed in the Middle East or Western Asia.
According to Heller, Eliezer was the first to print books in the Land of Israel.
According to Israel in Their Land, the historical significance of the press remains immense.

According to the blog, only in 1977, four hundred years after its appearance, was a facsimile edition of 'Lekach Tov' issued to mark the anniversary of the first Hebrew book printed in the Land of Israel.
According to the Jerusalem Post, when Israel Bak set up a printing press in Safed in 1832, he revived printing in the town after a hiatus of 245 years.
According to Heller, in the colophon of the mahzor Kashti retracted his earlier complaints and expressed criticism of Eliezer.
According to Heller, this criticism is softened by the fact that Kashti printed again with Eliezer, 'Lev Hakham', in 1586.
According to Heller, Eliezer copied ornamental material that other printers had used before him, a practice that was not uncommon at the time.
According to the Times of Israel blog, 'Lekach Tov' itself attracted relatively little interest, and its copies remained rare for centuries.

disagreements.question: In what year did Eliezer move to Safed?

versions.says: Encyclopaedia Judaica: in 1576, the same year in which he printed 'Mekor Barukh'
Israel in Their Land website: in 1577

disagreements.question: Who was Abraham ben Isaac, the partner in Safed?

versions.says: Marvin Heller: apparently not a relative, but a resident of Safed whom Eliezer had met in Constantinople
Joseph Rivlin, as cited by Heller: the press was founded by two brothers, Eleazer and Abraham ben Isaac

disagreements.question: How old was Yom Tov Tzahalon when he wrote 'Lekach Tov'?

versions.says: The Times of Israel blog: only about eighteen

disagreements.question: Was the Safed press the first in all of Asia?

versions.says: Marvin Heller: it was the first press not only in the Middle East but in all of Asia, excluding Chinese imprints

The Times of Israel blog: the claim, found in older popular accounts, that 'Lekach Tov' is the first book printed on the Asian continent is more problematic, since there was non-Hebrew printing in other regions

disagreements.question: Was the Safed press the first Hebrew press in the Middle East?

versions.says: Marvin Heller: it was the first press in the Middle East
Encyclopaedia Judaica: Gershom Soncino had already printed in Cairo, Egypt, in 1557, twenty years earlier

disagreements.question: When did Rabbi Yom Tov Tzahalon die?

versions.says: The Times of Israel blog: after 1638

claims.text: לפי הלר, ג'וזף ריבלין סבר אחרת: שבית הדפוס הוקם על ידי שני אחים, אלעזר ואברהם בן יצחק.
claims.quote: founded by two brothers, Eleazer and Abraham ben Isaac

claims.text: לפי הבלוג, צהלון היה בן כשמונה עשרה בלבד כשכתב את 'לקח טוב'.

claims.text: לפי הבלוג, הטענה בתיאורים פופולריים ישנים שזה הספר הראשון שנדפס ביבשת אסיה בעייתית יותר, לנוכח דפוס שאינו עברי באזורים אחרים.
